democracy: A system where the people choose who governs them, usually by voting, and can vote them out again.
autocracy: A system where one person or a small group holds power, and ordinary people can't remove them by voting.
parliament: A group of people who meet to make a country's laws, usually elected. Different countries call it different things, like Congress or the Diet.
parliamentary: A system where voters elect a parliament, and the parliament then decides who runs the government.
presidential: A system where the president is chosen separately from the people who write the laws, and runs the government. Most often voters elect the president, directly or through a special group of electors.
semi-presidential: A system with both a president and a prime minister who share power. Voters usually elect the president.
republic: A country where the head of state is chosen, not born into the job.
monarchy: A country with a king, queen, emperor or similar ruler who usually inherits the title.
constitutional monarchy: A country that keeps a king or queen as head of state, while the monarch's powers are limited by law and elected politicians usually do the governing.
absolute monarchy: A country where the monarch holds most of the power, and isn't limited by elected officials.
constitution: The top set of rules for a country. It says who has what power, and other laws have to follow it.
prime minister: The leader of the government in many countries. Usually chosen by parliament or the ruling party rather than directly by voters.
president: A leader who may either run the government or be mostly ceremonial, depending on the country.
chancellor: The title for the head of government in Germany and Austria, like a prime minister.
head of state: The person who officially represents the country, like a president or monarch. In some places the job is mostly symbolic, and in others it comes with real power.
head of government: The person who actually runs the government day to day.
coalition: When several parties team up to govern, because none won enough seats alone.
opposition: The parties that aren't in government, whose job includes questioning and challenging those that are. In some countries they have little freedom to do this.
plurality: The most votes of anyone, even if it's less than half.
cabinet: The group of senior ministers who run the big government departments.
minister: A senior politician in charge of one area of government, like health or defense.
legislature: The part of government that makes the laws.
upper house: In a parliament with two chambers, the second chamber. It often reviews laws and often represents regions, but its powers differ a lot between countries.
lower house: In a parliament with two chambers, the one that is usually larger and usually more powerful. It is usually elected directly.
senate: A name often used for the upper chamber of a parliament. Some senators are elected, and some are appointed.
unicameral: A parliament with just one chamber.
federal: A system where power is shared between the national government and states or provinces, each with powers of their own.
unitary: A system where the national government holds most power, and regions only have what it gives them.
proportional representation: A voting system where parties get seats in proportion to their votes. Win 30% of the votes, get about 30% of the seats.
first-past-the-post: A voting system where whoever gets the most votes in an area wins its seat, even without a majority.
two-round: A voting system where, if nobody gets a majority in the first vote, the top candidates face each other in a second vote.
runoff: A second vote between the top candidates, held when nobody won enough the first time.
ranked choice: A voting system where you rank candidates in order, and your vote moves to your next choice if your first is eliminated.
mixed-member: A voting system that combines local district winners with seats given out by party list. Sometimes the list seats make the result more proportional, and sometimes they don't.
party list: A ranked list of a party's candidates. If a party wins ten seats, the top ten people on its list get them.
threshold: The minimum share of votes a party needs before it gets any seats.
constituency: An area whose voters elect their own representative. Also called a district, electorate or riding.
electoral college: A group of people chosen to formally pick a leader. The US has 538 electors who choose the president, and in most states all of a state's electors go to whoever wins that state. Other countries use electoral colleges too.
midterm: In the US, elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, for Congress and many state offices.
gerrymandering: Drawing election district borders to help one side win more seats.
referendum: A vote where the people directly decide on a single question, instead of choosing a person.
junta: A government run by a small group of military officers, usually after they took power by force.
coup: A sudden, illegal takeover of government, often by the military.
one-party state: A country where one political party holds all real power, and other parties are banned or only allowed as junior partners.
theocracy: A government where religious leaders or religious law hold the highest authority.
dictatorship: Rule by one person with no real limits on their power.
independence: When a place stops being ruled by another country and governs itself.
colony: A territory ruled by a distant country, which is often used for its land and resources.
civil war: A war between groups within the same country.
sharia: Islamic religious law, which some countries use as part of their legal system.
tribal: Relating to traditional groups based on family ties and shared ancestry.
impeachment: A formal process in which a legislature accuses a top official of serious wrongdoing, which can lead to removal from office.
canton: A Swiss state. Swiss cantons have a lot of power of their own.
compulsory voting: When the law requires eligible people to vote, sometimes with a small fine if they don't.
incumbent: The person who currently holds an office and is trying to keep it in the next election.
ballot: The paper or screen where a voter marks their choice, or the act of voting itself.
delegate: A person chosen to speak and vote for a larger group, such as at a party meeting that picks a candidate.
veto: The power to say no to a decision or law so that it can't go ahead. In some countries it can be overridden.
caucus: A meeting of party members to choose candidates or make decisions. The word can also mean a group of politicians from one party or with a shared aim.
primary: A vote within a party to choose its candidate for an election. Primaries are used in the US and a few other places.
swing: A shift in votes from one party to another between elections. A swing seat or state is one that could go either way.
turnout: The share of eligible voters who actually vote in an election.
candidate: A person who is trying to win an election.
seat: One place in a parliament or other elected body. A party that wins 30 seats has 30 members there.
ceremonial: A role that's mostly for big occasions and symbols, without real power over decisions.
governor general: The person who stands in for the British monarch in countries like Canada and Australia. The role is mostly ceremonial.
federation: A country made up of states or provinces that each have powers of their own.
protectorate: A place that keeps its own rulers while a stronger country controls its defense and foreign affairs.
interim: Temporary. An interim leader holds the job until a permanent one is chosen.
hereditary: Passed down through a family, from parent to child.
sectarian: Divided along the lines of religious groups.
cleric: A religious leader, such as a priest or imam.
emir: A ruler in some Arab countries, a bit like a king.
sultan: A ruler in some Muslim countries, a bit like a king.
martial law: When the army takes over running things, usually in an emergency, and normal rights are put on hold.
term limit: A rule on how long or how many times someone can hold a job.
far right: A label for parties well to the right of most others, often very strict on immigration and national identity. Many parties given this label reject it.
far left: A label for parties well to the left of most others, often wanting big changes to who owns what. Many parties given this label reject it.
filibuster: Talking or using the rules to delay a vote in a lawmaking body, so a bill can't pass unless enough members agree to end the delay.
supreme court: The highest court in a country. It settles the hardest legal questions, and in many countries it can strike down laws that break the constitution.
voting age: How old you have to be to vote. In most countries it's 18, and in some it's 16 or 17.
